food.notes: Meal was eaten. User plated the food and used a knife and fork, reported that eating this way felt very enjoyable, and spent about 30 minutes on eating alone, which felt dramatically slower than their prior norm. Near the end, with a small piece of potato and some lettuce remaining, the user noticed they did not really want to keep eating those foods. They finished them anyway, then found they could still comfortably eat the remaining half dragon fruit. Afterward the user described fullness as gradual rather than an abrupt jump from not-full to very-full, and said the post-meal fruit felt unexpectedly pleasurable.

body_state.hunger: After lunch, user described a gradual, comfortable sense of fullness rather than a sudden transition to being very full. Around 17:50, user reported being hungry again. After dinner, user described the meal as more than intended.

context.learning_load: Google Calendar captured four code/study blocks with 220 minutes (3 h 40 min) of effective focus: 09:56-10:46, 15:17-16:53, 16:57-17:49, and 19:04-19:34. User felt this was less learning than desired.
context.stress_or_interruptions: User reported substantial unplanned phone use after lunch (roughly one to two hours by their estimate), more phone use after dinner, and another interruption when the 5 kg beef-rib delivery arrived and had to be fitted into the freezer, followed by more phone use. Calendar also explicitly captured a 21:00-22:00 Douyin + Xiaohongshu block.
context.other: User discovered they strongly enjoy eating plated meals with a knife and fork; the lunch took about 30 minutes of eating alone, a pace they described as previously unheard of for them. The user also discovered that eating fruit after the meal felt unexpectedly pleasurable. Dinner used available leftovers; the dish was spicy, which the user felt pushed intake upward and was followed by cooling/sweet foods. The 5 kg beef-rib delivery arrived later in the evening and created a practical storage interruption.

observed_patterns: Sleep duration was approximately 7 h 50 min.
Breakfast combined yogurt, oats, fruit, and egg rather than a single-food meal.
The first plated knife-and-fork lunch produced a clearly positive subjective response.
The plated lunch lasted about 30 minutes, substantially slower than the user's prior eating pace.
A meal-ending signal appeared before the plate was empty: the user no longer wanted the remaining potato and lettuce, while a different food (dragon fruit) still felt easy to eat afterward.
Post-meal fullness was experienced as a gradual ramp rather than an abrupt threshold.
The post-meal fruit added a strong positive sensory and emotional finish to the meal.
Hunger returned by about 17:50 after the midday meal.
At dinner, a spicy leftover dish coincided with eating nearly all available rice and leftovers, then adding watermelon and an ice pop.

Effective study time was 3 h 40 min according to the synced calendar blocks, but the user's subjective dissatisfaction came from large transition gaps rather than an inability to sustain long focused blocks.

Phone use repeatedly appeared at transition points: after meals and after an external interruption, suggesting that re-entry into the main task may be a more important bottleneck than focus duration once work has started.
uncertainties: Exact breakfast time was not reported.
It is not yet known whether the late-lunch loss of interest reflected physical fullness, sensory-specific satiety, preference for the fruit, or some combination.
Dinner amounts were described relative to what was available rather than weighed or measured.
Whether the previously considered egg was actually eaten at dinner was not confirmed.
Total phone-use duration cannot be reconstructed exactly from the calendar because some reported phone use was not separately logged.
exploratory_questions: Is the main learning bottleneck on independent-living days the duration of focused blocks, or the probability of returning to work after meals and interruptions?
What is the smallest reliable 'resume cue' after lunch or an interruption that gets the user back into the previous task before the phone captures the transition?
Does putting a clear next action on screen before leaving the desk reduce post-meal re-entry friction?
When a meal is spicy, does the user tend to eat more starch specifically to buffer the heat, and then seek cold or sweet foods afterward?
Does a 25-30 minute meal remain natural once the novelty of the plate-and-utensil setup fades?
next_observations: Notice the first 10-20 minutes after meals and external interruptions: whether the phone appears automatically and how easy it is to reopen the exact prior task.
Notice whether leaving a concrete next step before a break changes re-entry speed.
Continue observing gradual fullness and meal-ending signals without turning them into a score or quota.
